explanations.explanation: Paul says, “But you, O man of God, flee from these things…” (1 Timothy 6:11). He's just finished warning about the love of money, so these things are what Timothy is supposed to run from. FLEE, friend. I've been stuck in a drawer, and I can tell you nobody sprints away from something and also keeps one eye on it.

That would be a nice, calm evening class, but it's not what Paul wrote. He says to flee from these things, right after warning about the love of money. Nobody takes notes while running for the door. Class is dismissed, friend, and so is the notebook.

Profit from these things? Paul had just said that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10). So he's not handing Timothy a business opportunity. He says flee, and he means it. I've got a lot of ideas, but cashing in on the thing Paul says to run from isn't one of them.

Paul says to “pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness.” Notice the two directions. Flee from the money trap, and pursue this list. Same legs, different direction, friend, and I'd say the second direction is the better workout.

Teaching does come up in this letter, but not here. Paul's word for this list is pursue. He wants Timothy chasing righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance and gentleness, not putting them on a lesson plan. Pursuing is running toward something.

Studying sounds sensible, but Paul picked a different word. He says to pursue these things. That's less like sitting at a desk and more like chasing something down the street with your apron flapping. I know which one burns more cookie calories.

Paul says, “Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called…” (1 Timothy 6:12). Timothy was called to it. So he's told to grab hold of it, like you'd grab a rope you were just thrown. Eternal is a lot longer than any batch I've ever baked.

Earthly life is the one we're all living now, but that's not the word Paul uses. He says the life Timothy was called to is eternal life. Paul points Timothy past what's right in front of him. Earthly would be a smaller prize than the one Paul has in mind.
Look at the sentence right before it. Paul says, “Fight the good fight of the faith.” Nobody calls a fight easy, friend. Paul wrote eternal life, and I'd say the word easy was never even invited.
Paul says the opposite. He says Timothy made the good confession “before many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12). That's a whole crowd, not an empty room. So there were people there to hear it.

Right. Paul says Timothy made the good confession “before many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12). Many, friend. That's a full room, and I think it's the kind of moment where you remember who was standing there.

Paul says Christ Jesus “made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.” Pilate was the governor who held Jesus' trial (Matthew 27:2). So Paul points Timothy to Jesus' own example. Timothy confessed before many witnesses, and Jesus stood before the governor.

Felix was a governor (Acts 23:24), so I see where your head went. But Paul names someone else here. In verse 13 it's Pontius Pilate, the governor who held Jesus' trial (Matthew 27:2). Two governors, one name in the verse, friend.

Agrippa was a king (Acts 25:13), but Paul doesn't name him in this verse. The name Paul gives is Pontius Pilate. He was the governor Jesus stood before (Matthew 27:2). A king and a governor are easy to mix up, so no worries.

Paul says to keep the commandment “without stain or reproach until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ.” So Timothy keeps going until Jesus appears. No finish line he can set for himself. It's a keep-the-oven-on kind of job.
That sounds reasonable, and plenty of jobs work that way. But Paul sets a different finish line. It's until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ. His own to-do list doesn't set the end date.

Paul had urged Timothy to stay in Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3), so I see where that comes from. But no city shows up in this verse. Paul says to keep the commandment until the appearance of our Lord Jesus Christ. Where Timothy is standing doesn't change that.

No date shows up anywhere here. Paul says the Sovereign One “will bring about” that appearance “in His own time” (1 Timothy 6:15). Jesus Himself says no one knows that day or hour except the Father (Matthew 24:36). I don't hand out dates either.

Right. Paul gives no date. He says the Sovereign One will bring it about “in His own time” (1 Timothy 6:15). Jesus says nobody knows the day or hour except the Father (Matthew 24:36). So no circling dates on the calendar, friend.

Paul says it plainly: “No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him.” He says it right after saying that the Sovereign One dwells in unapproachable light. It's a LOT of light, friend. Even my ovens don't come close.

Paul actually says it: “No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him.” That comes right after he says the Sovereign One dwells in unapproachable light. So True was the answer. It's a different kind of glow than my ovens put out.

Paul finishes with, “To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.” After saying who the Sovereign One is, he can't help but praise Him. I think that's what happens when you really look at who He is. You say Amen.
Paul does give Timothy a warning later, in verse 20. But that's not how this part ends. He closes verse 16 with praise: “To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.”
No names show up here. Paul's last words in this part are “To Him be honor and eternal dominion! Amen.” He finishes with praise. Short, strong and to the point.

Paul says to put hope “in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy.” Wealth can't hold that kind of hope. God can. I like the sound of that, because my own hopes got a lot safer once they left that drawer.
Wisdom is a good thing to have, friend. But Paul says the rich should put their hope in God. He's the one Paul says richly provides all things for us to enjoy. Wisdom isn't the name in that verse.

Family matters a lot to me, believe me. But it isn't the answer in this verse. Paul says the rich should put their hope in God, not in wealth. He's the one who richly provides all things for us to enjoy.
Paul calls it “the uncertainty of wealth.” That's why the hope goes in God instead. Money can be here today and gone before the cookies cool. Paul says it's uncertain, and I'd say that's honest.
Paul actually uses the word. He says not to put hope in “the uncertainty of wealth.” So wealth is the uncertain one in this verse. That's why Paul points the rich to God instead.
Paul tells Timothy to instruct the rich “to do good, to be rich in good works.” See what he did there? Same word, new meaning. Rich in good works. That's a bank account I can get behind.
Mercy is a lovely thing to be full of, but Paul's word in this verse is different. He says to be rich in good works. That's doing good, not just feeling it. The rich get something to DO.

Faith matters a great deal in this letter, friend. But in this verse Paul says to be rich in good works. He pairs it with doing good and being generous and ready to share. So the answer here is good works.
Paul says to be “generous and ready to share.” Ready is the word I like. Not “eventually.” Like the guy who's already got the cookie box open when you walk in.
Saving has its place, but it's not the word Paul uses here. He says to be generous and ready to share. Ready to save would be somebody guarding the cookie jar. Paul wants the opposite.

Waiting is how a lot of us spend our time, but Paul isn't asking for that. He says to be generous and ready to share. Ready to wait is just a person at a bus stop. Paul wants someone ready to hand something over.

explanations.answer: A firm foundation for the future
explanations.explanation: Paul says they are “treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future.” Giving feels like losing something, but Paul says it builds something. It's a foundation, friend, the part of the bakery nobody sees but everything stands on. I'd call that a smart investment.

explanations.answer: A good name in the city
explanations.explanation: A good name sounds nice, and I'd like one too. But Paul never mentions it here. What he says they treasure up is “a firm foundation for the future.” That's the part that holds everything else up.

Neighbors are great, but they're not in Paul's sentence. He says the generous are “treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future.” The text doesn't say why anyone's neighbors come into it. The foundation is what Paul names.

Paul says to avoid “irreverent, empty chatter” and the opposing arguments of so-called “knowledge.” That's the stuff that sounds smart but doesn't hold anything. A lot of talk can be like dough with no flour in it. It looks like something and then there's nothing there.

Those don't show up in this letter's last words. Paul tells Timothy to avoid “irreverent, empty chatter” and the opposing arguments of so-called “knowledge.” It's about talk, not parties. Still a good thing to dodge.

Paul did just talk about the rich, so it's easy to see why that pops up. But he doesn't tell Timothy to avoid them. He says to avoid “irreverent, empty chatter” and the opposing arguments of so-called “knowledge.” Fine clothes are safe, even my apron.

Paul says the opposite. Of this so-called “knowledge,” he says, “…which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith.” Some did. That's why he tells Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him.
Right. Paul says some have professed this so-called “knowledge” and “thus swerved away from the faith.” Swerved, like a car drifting out of its lane. That's why he told Timothy to avoid it.
Paul closes with, “Grace be with you all.” After all that fighting, guarding and fleeing, the last word is grace. I like how that lands. It's like the last batch coming out warm.
Peace is a lovely blessing, and Paul uses it in other places. But he doesn't use it here. His last words in this letter are “Grace be with you all.”
Timothy could use some strength after that list, and I'd bet he'd say so too. But Paul doesn't end with it. His closing blessing is “Grace be with you all.” Grace, and that's the final word.
